We need to tell Cuple about the server's location. Since the client has no way to get the specified path information without a code generator, currently every request goes to one path (usually /rpc) with the desired HTTP method. // cuple.ts import { createClient } from "@cuple/client"; import type { routes } from "../backend/src/app"; export const client = createClient<typeof routes>({ path: "http://localhost:8080/rpc", });

import { fetchCuple } from "@cuple/client"; async function getPost(id: number) { // Resolves with success; any other result throws. const { post } = await fetchCuple(client.getPost.get, { params: { id } }); return post; } async function findPost(id: number) { // A failure you handle is listed, and typed. const res = await fetchCuple(client.getPost.get, { params: { id } }).thenResolveAlso([ "not-found-error", ]); return res.result === "not-found-error" ? null : res.post; } See Handling results. Why it works this way No code generator. A generated client is only as fresh as its last generation; forget that step, and the client compiles against an old API. Here the types come from typeof routes, so a server change is a client type error as soon as you save. One RPC path. Without generated code, the client can't know each route's URL, so requests name the route on one path (/rpc). Routes with .path() are still plain REST for other clients.

fetchCuple resolves with success. Anything else rejects: import { fetchCuple } from "@cuple/client"; const { user } = await fetchCuple(client.getUser.get, { params: { id } }); Outcome Rejects with Any other result: a 404, a validation-error CupleUnexpectedResponseError, with the response No answer: offline, DNS, CORS, a proxy's HTML error page CupleTransportError signal aborted DOMException (AbortError)

When your code has something to do with a failure, list it. It resolves as a typed value instead of rejecting: const res = await fetchCuple(client.createUser.post, { body }).thenResolveAlso([ "validation-error", ]); // ^? success | validation-error if (res.result === "validation-error") showIssues(res.issues); Anything you didn't list still rejects, so there's no case you forgot to check. "transport-error" can be listed like any result, for code that has something to do when the server can't be reached (a form that keeps the user's input). It resolves as { result: "transport-error", statusCode, message }. statusCode is set when something answered, but not in Cuple's format (a gateway page).

Method Resolves with .thenResolveAlso([...]) success, plus the listed results .thenResolveOn([...]) exactly the listed results; "success" is not implied .thenResolveAll() every result the server sent, for code that forwards responses as they are (a proxy, an MCP tool) .thenWrapAbort() adds an abort, as { result: "abort" } const res = await fetchCuple(client.search.get, { query, options: { signal } }).thenWrapAbort(); if (res.result === "abort") return; // a newer search replaced this one

@cuple/react follows the same rule: useGet gives you success, and { resolveAlso: [...] } lists what the component renders instead. Inside useAction, use thenResolveAlso. Whatever nobody listed goes to the nearest <Boundary>. See Errors. Why it works this way The common case is success. Most calls have nothing to do with a failure except show it somewhere generic, so checking result === "success" at every call site is noise, and forgetting it hands an error to code that expects data. A failure you handle is typed. Listing it puts it in the return type, so TypeScript checks you handle it, with its real shape (issues on a validation error). A try/catch gives you unknown. One rule everywhere. fetchCuple, useGet and useAction all start from success and widen by listing, so there's one habit to learn.

// Server: const routes = { foo: builder.get(/**/), bar: builder.post(/**/), baz: builder.put(/**/), qux: builder.patch(/**/), quux: builder.delete(/**/), }; // Client: await fetchCuple(client.foo.get); await fetchCuple(client.bar.post); await fetchCuple(client.baz.put); await fetchCuple(client.qux.patch); await fetchCuple(client.quux.delete);

Since Cuple doesn't have a code generator, you have to tell the HTTP method in order to build up the fetch request with the right method. It's type-checked so you cannot specify methods other than what the server specifies.

documents.t: body: The request body headers: HTTP headers params: URL parameters (e.g.: in case of /post/:id, it can be { id: "1" }) query: query parameters (e.g.: in case of ?id=2, it can be { id: "2" }) signal: an AbortSignal Every parameter's type is auto-infered from the server. await fetchCuple(client.user.updateUser.patch, { body: { name: 'David' }, headers: { authorization: 'Bearer ...' }, params: { id: 12 }, query: { 'foo': 'bar' } })

The server's route declares every result it can send, and the client knows them all: // What client.getPosts.get can answer: | { result: "success"; statusCode: 200; posts: Post[] } | { result: "unexpected-error"; statusCode: 500; message: string } fetchCuple resolves with the success one and rejects the others, unless you list them. See Handling results. Why it works this way The method is written at the call site. client.createTodo.post says on the wire and in review that this call changes data, and it's what lets useGet refuse writes by type.

Every behavior is set through one config object, grouped by concern. The same shape is accepted in three places: <CupleProvider store={store} config={appConfig}> // the app's defaults <Boundary config={{ cache: { keep: 0 } }}> // everything inside this region <Report /> // useGet(client.report, args, { config: { ... } }) </Boundary> </CupleProvider> Each setting cascades on its own: the request's wins over the Boundary's, over the provider's, over the built-in default. Setting cache.keep on a Boundary never resets cache.refreshOnRead from the provider.

Setting Default What it does keep 5 minutes How long data nobody reads stays in memory. 0 drops it as soon as the last reader unmounts: for large data. With several readers, the longest wins. refreshOnRead "stale" A component starts reading data that's already cached (another tab, a reopened panel): it shows at once, and "stale" refetches it in the background if it's older than freshFor. "always" always does, "never" never does. A first load is never fetched twice: "coming back" means some component has read this data before. freshFor 0 How long data counts as fresh for "stale", in ms. onKeyChange "drop" What store.refreshKeys() does with data whose key changed: "drop" deletes it at once, "keep" keeps it for keep, so switching back is instant: only when one person owns every account, since the old account's data shows again at once. Read from the provider.

Setting Default What it does unhandled "boundary" Actions: where an error nobody handled goes. "boundary", "notify", or a function choosing per CupleError. See Errors. notify none How the app shows an error without replacing the page, given a CupleError. Used by "notify" and <Boundary error="notify">. message "Something went wrong." The CupleError message when there's nothing more readable: a network failure, a server result without a message, a bug in production.

Setting Default What it does blocking false Counts for useIsFetching({ blocking: true }): actions while they run, reads while their data refetches. For a full-page overlay. See The store. every none Reads only: refetch every this many ms while something reads it.

useGet, usePages: cache, loading. useAction: errors, loading.blocking. <Boundary error>: errors.message; with "notify", errors.notify. Plain code on the store (store.preload, store.refreshKeys): the provider's config. Why it works this way The same config in three places. A setting often needs to change for one region (a report that should drop its data when it's closed) or one request. With one shape at every level, moving a setting from a request to a region is a copy-paste, not a different API. Each setting cascades on its own. A region that only changes keep shouldn't reset the app's refreshOnRead. Merging per setting keeps overrides small.

/** * Puts the server's validation errors on the form's fields. Here the request * body has the form's shape, so an issue's path is the field's name * (`["address", "zip"]` → `address.zip`). When the shapes differ, translate the * path here. An issue without a path goes to the form as a whole. */ function showServerIssues<T extends FieldValues>( form: UseFormReturn<T>, issues: ServerIssue[], ) { issues.forEach((issue, i) => { const error = { type: "server", message: issue.message }; if (issue.path.length === 0) form.setError("root.server", error); else form.setError(issue.path.join(".") as FieldPath<T>, error, { shouldFocus: i === 0, }); }); } An issue's path is the field's name, nested ones included: ["address", "zip"] becomes address.zip. Rules only the server can check (an email already in use) come back the same way, so the form needs no special case for them.

Every failure is either handled or unhandled. Handled means your code listed it: thenResolveAlso(["validation-error"]) on a request, resolveAlso: ["not-found-error"] on a read. It comes back as a typed value, and the component renders it like any data. Unhandled is everything else: a result nobody listed, a network failure nobody listed, a bug. It goes to the nearest <Boundary>, as a CupleError with a message that is always readable. const save = useAction(async (values: ContactValues) => { const response = await fetchCuple(client.updateContact.put, { params: { id }, body: values }) .thenResolveAlso(["validation-error", "transport-error"]); // ^? success | validation-error | transport-error — all typed if (response.result === "validation-error") showIssues(response.issues); if (response.result === "transport-error") showOffline(); return response; }); // A 403, a 500, a bug: unhandled. The nearest <Boundary> shows error.message.

Any result the endpoint can return can be listed, and so can "transport-error": no answer from the server at all (offline, DNS, a proxy's error page). Listing makes it part of the return type, so TypeScript checks you handle every case you listed, and nothing else reaches your code. On Write A request fetchCuple(...).thenResolveAlso(["validation-error", "transport-error"]) A read useGet(client.getNote, args, { resolveAlso: ["not-found-error"] }) A read inside combine get(client.getOrder, args, { resolveAlso: ["not-found-error"] }) type TransportErrorResult = { result: "transport-error"; statusCode: number | null; message: string };

A read that fails with something unlisted goes to the nearest <Boundary>. When a region can go without its data, let the boundary notify instead, and show nothing: <Boundary fallback={<Skeleton width="10rem" />} error="notify"> <Header /> </Boundary> For a failure that is a normal outcome (a deleted item), list it with resolveAlso and render it. See Reading. NOTE: "notify" needs config.errors.notify. Without it, the error goes to the boundary above, saying what's missing. Why it works this way List what you handle, instead of catching it. catch (error) gives you unknown: a validation error's issues have to be narrowed out by hand, and a typo in a result name still compiles. A listed result is in the return type, with its real shape. Unhandled errors go to a boundary by default. An error kept in action.error that no component renders is an error nobody sees. Sending it where a failed read goes makes the default visible; "notify" is a choice you make where it fits. One CupleError with a message. The boundary is written once, for every kind of failure. Given raw errors, it would need to know about results, network errors and bugs. And a bug's own message can leak internals, so in production it's replaced by errors.message.

Infinite-query caches have their own rules for refetching and invalidation. Here a page is a normal read, so refresh: [client.getNotes] refreshes the loaded pages like any other read, and follows cursors that moved when an item was deleted.

npm i @cuple/react @cuple/client Requires React 19. @cuple/react is fetchCuple with memory: Reading: cache what fetchCuple returns and suspend while loading. Writing: run your own async function. You get its state, its errors, and a refresh of exactly what it changed. Cached data changes only when: an action that names it finishes, refresh() is called, a poll fires, or an entry nobody reads expires. Nothing refetches on focus, on mount, or on a timer you didn't ask for.

Create the store next to your client. Plain code, like sign-in or an SSE handler, uses it directly: /** The cache. One per app; plain code (sign-in, SSE handlers) uses it directly. */ export const store = createCupleStore(); /** What each write changes, in one place. Actions name these in `refresh`. */ export const refreshes = { notes: [client.getNotes, client.getNote], contacts: [client.listContacts, client.getContact], }; // Switching accounts re-reads only what depends on the account: every call's // key changed, so each reader reads again under the new one. The previous // account's data is dropped at once (the default `onKeyChange: "drop"`): the // next person at this screen may not be the same person. export function signIn(accountId: AccountId) { signedInAs = accountId; store.refreshKeys(); } // Signing out drops everything: nothing of the account stays in memory. export function signOut() { signedInAs = null; store.clear(); } Then provide it once, at the root: export const store = createCupleStore(); const config: CupleConfig = { errors: { // How the app shows an error without replacing the page. notify: (error) => alert(error.message), // An error no code handled: a dropped connection keeps the page, // anything else goes to the nearest . unhandled: (error) => (error.kind === "transport" ? "notify" : "boundary"), }, }; export function App() { return ( } error={(error, retry) => (

{error.message}{" "}

)} > ); } In this example: config.errors.notify is how the app shows an error without replacing the page. config.errors.unhandled decides, per error nobody handled, whether it's shown with it ("notify") or goes to the nearest ("boundary", the default). See Errors and Configuration. is a and an error boundary in one. error.message is always readable; retry drops what failed and renders again. refreshes lists what each write changes, in one place. See Actions.

First loads suspend: give <Boundary fallback> a skeleton shaped like the content, so nothing jumps when the data lands. Refreshes keep the content on screen; show background work with useIsFetching(), e.g. a thin bar at the top. Actions show where they act: mark the button or row with aria-busy={action.isPending} and style it. Delay placeholders by about 150 ms with CSS (animation-delay), so fast responses never flash one. The example app in examples/react does all three.

The cache doesn't know what your client's middleware sends, so tell it whose data a call is, with a key: /** The cache. One per app; plain code (sign-in, SSE handlers) uses it directly. */ export const store = createCupleStore(); /** What each write changes, in one place. Actions name these in `refresh`. */ export const refreshes = { notes: [client.getNotes, client.getNote], contacts: [client.listContacts, client.getContact], }; // Switching accounts re-reads only what depends on the account: every call's // key changed, so each reader reads again under the new one. The previous // account's data is dropped at once (the default `onKeyChange: "drop"`): the // next person at this screen may not be the same person. export function signIn(accountId: AccountId) { signedInAs = accountId; store.refreshKeys(); } // Signing out drops everything: nothing of the account stays in memory. export function signOut() { signedInAs = null; store.clear(); } key is read when a call is cached. store.refreshKeys() checks every cached call's key again: unchanged ones stay, changed ones are read again under the new key. Components re-read even when memoized. By default (cache.onKeyChange: "drop"), the previous account's data is deleted at once, so nothing of it can show again. "keep" keeps it for cache.keep, so switching back is instant (and refreshes in the background). Use it only for an account switcher where one person owns every account, like work and personal inboxes. When a different person can sign in on the same screen, keep the default. Signing out calls store.clear(): nothing of the account stays in memory.

import { mockCuple, renderWithCuple } from "@cuple/react/testing"; const mock = mockCuple<typeof routes>({ getTodos: { get: () => ({ result: "success", statusCode: 200, todos: ["milk"] }) }, }); vi.stubGlobal("fetch", mock.fetch); await renderWithCuple(<Boundary fallback="loading"><Todos /></Boundary>); expect(await screen.findByText("milk")).toBeDefined(); renderWithCuple renders under a provider with a fresh store, inside the awaited act React 19 needs for Suspense. Plain render never leaves the fallback. mockCuple is a fake server typed from your routes: a handler returning the wrong shape, or for an endpoint that doesn't exist, is a type error. A request with no handler fails with the endpoint's name. mock.calls records every request. In a monorepo you can test against the real routes instead: run the server in the test, and point the client at it. Why it works this way Most data bugs are timing bugs. A screen that refetches on window focus, on mount or on a timer changes while the user is reading it, and the bug report says "sometimes the list jumps back". Here, cached data changes only for a reason written in the code: an action's refresh, a poll you configured, a call to the store. A store you create, not a hidden global. Sign-in, an SSE handler and a router loader aren't components, but they need to refresh or clear data. They use the same store the hooks use, and each test can start from a fresh one.

The server has these routes: export const routes = { getTodos: builder.get(async () => success({ todos })), createTodo: builder .bodySchema(z.strictObject({ text: z.string().min(1, "Write something first.") })) .post(async ({ data }) => { if (todos.some((todo) => todo.text === data.body.text)) { return zodValidationError([ { code: "custom", path: ["text"], message: "You already have this todo." }, ]); } const todo = { id: todos.length + 1, text: data.body.text, done: false }; todos.push(todo); return success({ todo }); }), toggleTodo: builder .paramsSchema(z.strictObject({ id: z.number() })) .patch(async ({ data }) => { const todo = todos.find((todo) => todo.id === data.params.id)!; todo.done = !todo.done; return success({ todo }); }), clearCompleted: builder.post(async () => { todos = todos.filter((todo) => !todo.done); return success({}); }), };

Both the schema's error and the custom one are validation-error, with path: ["text"]. create.value is what the function returned, typed, so the form can show the issue next to the input. refresh: { success: [...] } names what the action changes, and when: the todos are refetched only when one was created. Nothing else is.

status Meaning idle Nothing has happened yet. pending Running, including the refresh it asked for. The screen keeps the old data until the new data lands. done Your function finished. value is what it returned, including failures you listed, so check value.result. failed Your function threw something nobody handled, and errors.unhandled is "notify". error is the CupleError. run never rejects. It resolves with the resulting state, so it can go straight into a form library's submit handler.

Nothing is refreshed unless the action names it. List what a write changes. When the server computes one thing from another (property cards counting permits), list both: /** The cache. One per app; plain code (sign-in, SSE handlers) uses it directly. */ export const store = createCupleStore(); /** What each write changes, in one place. Actions name these in `refresh`. */ export const refreshes = { notes: [client.getNotes, client.getNote], contacts: [client.listContacts, client.getContact], }; // Switching accounts re-reads only what depends on the account: every call's // key changed, so each reader reads again under the new one. The previous // account's data is dropped at once (the default `onKeyChange: "drop"`): the // next person at this screen may not be the same person. export function signIn(accountId: AccountId) { signedInAs = accountId; store.refreshKeys(); } // Signing out drops everything: nothing of the account stays in memory. export function signOut() { signedInAs = null; store.clear(); } /** One action per row, so each row has its own pending state. */ function NoteRow(props: { note: { id: number; text: string }; onOpen: (id: number) => void; }) { const remove = useAction( () => fetchCuple(client.deleteNote.delete, { params: { id: props.note.id }, }), // A failed row action shouldn't take the page with it. { refresh: refreshes.notes, config: { errors: { unhandled: "notify" } } }, ); return (
  • remove.run()} > Delete
    • ); } Every cached call of a listed endpoint is refetched, and so is every combine that read one of them through get. Only calls something is reading are refetched. The rest are dropped, and fetched fresh when next read. So when you delete the note an open pane shows, and close the pane inside the action, the deleted note is never refetched and never 404s. refresh: [...] refreshes every time the function finishes. refresh: { success: [...] } refreshes only for the listed results, as NewTodo above does; the keys are typed from what the function returns.

Errors you handle are results you list with thenResolveAlso, "transport-error" included: typed values in value. Anything else your function throws (a result it didn't list, a network failure it didn't list, a bug) is unhandled, and config.errors.unhandled decides where it goes: per action, per <Boundary>, or app-wide on the provider: "boundary": the nearest <Boundary>, as a CupleError. The default. "notify": config.errors.notify shows it; the page stays, and the status becomes failed. Errors never end up only in the console. See Errors for all the cases in one app.

When a component moves to another item, give it a key (key={note.id}), or it shows the previous item's result. The state is the latest run's. An earlier run that finishes later still writes and refreshes, but doesn't change what is shown. Steps that must all happen or none belong in one server route. The client can sequence steps, but it can't make them a transaction. Why it works this way Your own function, not a mutation config. Real writes are sequences: save, then upload, then navigate. Split into mutationFn, onSuccess and onError options, the order things run in becomes something to look up. An async function reads top to bottom. A refresh list, not automatic invalidation. Invalidation by guessed keys either misses something (a stale screen) or refetches everything (a slow one), and neither shows in the code. A list next to the write can be reviewed, and a missing entry shows up as stale data the first time you try it. run never rejects. A rejected promise in an onClick is an unhandled rejection that only reaches the console, and a form library awaiting a rejected submit can leave isSubmitting stuck. Errors go to a boundary or notify instead. The latest run wins. Two quick clicks on a slow network can finish in either order; showing whichever finished last could show the older result.

Events are not stored: you decide what to keep, and what to refresh. store.refresh(...) refetches what's on screen when someone else changed it. The connection is closed when the component unmounts, and opened again when the arguments change. A rejected connection (e.g. 401) throws to the nearest , like a failed read. A network failure is kept as error, with isStreaming: false: streams drop, and the page should stay. reconnect() tries again. StreamEvent gives you the event type from the server. Why it works this way Events aren't kept. A stream is a series of changes, not a value; kept in memory, it grows forever. Usually an event means "something changed", and refreshing the reads it affects keeps one source of truth for what's on screen. A rejected connection throws, a dropped one doesn't. A 401 won't fix itself, so it's an error for the boundary. A long-lived connection dropping is normal (a laptop going to sleep), so it's state the component shows while you reconnect.
The store is the cache. Components reach it through <CupleProvider>; plain code uses it directly.

await store.refresh([client.getNotes, client.getNote]); Calls something is reading are refetched, and keep their old data on screen until the new data lands. Calls nobody reads are dropped, and fetched fresh when next read. It resolves when the refetches have landed, and never rejects: a failure goes to whoever reads the data. A network failure during a refresh keeps the old data on screen, and is retried when the browser comes back online.

Start a fetch before anything renders it: <li onMouseEnter={() => store.preload(loadOrderWithCustomer, order.id)}> It never rejects, and a failed preload isn't kept: nobody was waiting for it, so the next read fetches again. In a router loader, call it without returning it (void store.preload(...)), so loading and errors stay with <Boundary> instead of the router. NOTE: A read of { id: 5 } doesn't hit a preload of { id: "5" }. When that happens, the store warns in the console.

signedInAs = "linus"; store.refreshKeys(); Checks every cached call's key again, for when whatever a with({ key }) getter returns has changed: Key unchanged: stays as it is. No request, no re-render. Key changed: its readers read again under the new key, even memoized ones. Cached data for the new key shows at once; anything else loads. The old key's data is dropped, or kept with cache.onKeyChange: "keep". It's never refetched under the new key. Combined reads built from a changed call run again; streams reconnect. Wrap it in startTransition to keep the current screen until the new data is ready.
store.clear(); Drops everything; readers suspend and fetch again. For sign-out and tests.

<Boundary fallback={<Spinner />} error={(error, retry) => <Failed onRetry={retry} />}> Without fallback, loading goes to the boundary above. Without error, errors go to the boundary above. retry drops the data that failed from the cache and renders again, so it's fetched fresh. Other data is untouched. Place boundaries where the layout wants loading and error UI: a failing widget shouldn't take the page with it.

Most loading should stay local: skeletons, busy buttons. For the few steps the user must wait for, opt in with loading: { blocking: true }, and cover the page only then: /** A bulk step the user must wait for: blocks the page while it runs. */ function ImportSamples() { const importSamples = useAction(() => fetchCuple(client.importContacts.post), { refresh: refreshes.contacts, config: { loading: { blocking: true }, errors: { unhandled: "notify" } }, }); return ( ); } /** * Covers the page while a blocking step runs: only work that asked for it with * `blocking: true`, never ordinary loads. */ export function PageOverlay() { const blocking = useIsFetching({ blocking: true }); if (!blocking) return null; return (

function Progress() { return useIsFetching() ? <TopBar /> : null; } True while any read, refresh or action runs. For a global progress bar. Why it works this way Refreshes keep the old data on screen. Swapping content for a spinner on every refetch makes the page jump under the user's cursor. The old data stays until the new data lands, and useIsFetching() says something is updating. Only what's read is refetched. Refetching every cached call of an endpoint spends requests on screens nobody is looking at, and refetching a deleted item 404s. Unread entries are dropped instead, and load fresh when they're read again. refreshKeys, not a clear. Clearing on an account switch refetches everything, including data that doesn't depend on the account, and flashes every skeleton at once. Re-reading only what the key changed keeps the rest.

For a list that should always render, a failure means something is broken. Every component that reads the same call shares one request and one cached result, so NewTodo and TodoItem don't need anything passed down.

Reads are GET only: a read runs on every render, refresh and poll, so a write endpoint (client.createTodo.post) is refused, by the types and at runtime. For a POST that only reads, like a search, wrap it: combine(async (_, q: string) => fetchCuple(client.search.post, { body: { q } })). A route stands for its GET endpoint: useGet(client.getNote, ...) is useGet(client.getNote.get, ...), and both are the same cached call. The short form works wherever something is read or refreshed: useGet, usePages, get inside combine, refresh lists, store.refresh and store.preload. NOTE: A route that is itself named like an HTTP method (client.get) needs .get written out: at runtime, that's the only way to tell a route from an endpoint.

A component reads useGet(client.getNote, { params: { id } }), and id changes: the user opened another note. What should it show while the new note loads? By default, the nearest shows its fallback again. The old note's text under the new note's title would be wrong, and a click on "Delete" in that moment would delete the note the user is no longer looking at. That's the wrong trade for a search box: every keystroke would blank the results and flash a skeleton, while the previous results are still useful for a moment. There, keep them on screen with React's useDeferredValue, and dim them so it's clear they're about to change: function SearchResults({ query }: { query: string }) { // Lags behind `query` until the results for the new query are ready. const deferred = useDeferredValue(query); const { results } = useGet(client.search, { query: { q: deferred } }); return (

The list already loaded each customer, so opening an order sends one request, getOrder, and Ada is fetched once even though she has two orders. OrderDetails suspends once, until both are there. Use await for a fetch that needs another's result, and Promise.all for independent ones. One failed get fails the whole read, and the shows it. To go on without it, list the result: get(client.getCustomer, args, { resolveAlso: ["not-found-error"] }). Refreshing client.getOrder or client.getCustomer re-runs loadOrderWithCustomer. NOTE: Create combined reads at module level: a combined read's identity is its cache key. Its arguments must be JSON (numbers, strings, plain objects and arrays), because they are part of the key too. To run it: cd examples/docs && npm run dev:orders.

const { count } = useGet(client.getStats, undefined, { config: { loading: { every: 30_000 } } }); It polls only while something reads it. When several readers poll the same data at different intervals, the shortest wins. Why it works this way Loading and errors belong to the layout. With isLoading and error in every component, each one draws its own spinner, and a page with five reads pops in five times. Components read data as if it's there, and a <Boundary> decides what the user sees meanwhile, for everything inside it. The call is the cache key. Hand-written keys (["order", id]) drift from the request: forget a parameter, and two different requests share one entry. Here the endpoint, the client's key and the arguments are the key, so they can't disagree. A read can run again at any time. Refreshes, polls and retries re-run it without asking. Only a request that's safe to repeat can be a read; a write repeated by a refresh would create a second record.

Please follow the steps in the comments. import express from "express"; import { z } from "zod"; import { createBuilder, initRpc } from "@cuple/server"; import { apiResponse, success } from "@cuple/server"; const app = express(); const builder = createBuilder(app); // STEP 1: Create builder with the express instance const posts = [ { id: 1, title: "Hi again", content: "This is my second post" }, { id: 2, title: "Hi", content: "This is my first post" }, ]; // STEP 2: Define some request handlers export const routes = { getPosts: builder.get(async () => { return success({ posts }); }), }; // STEP 3: Create the RPC handler (Required to use with @cuple/client) initRpc(app, { path: "/rpc", routes }); app.listen(8080, () => { console.log(`Example app listening on port 8080`); }); Why it works this way Express underneath. Logging, CORS, sessions and deployment stay as they are in an Express app; Cuple routes are added next to the ones you have. Routes are one exported object. Its type is the contract: the client, the OpenAPI generator and the MCP server all read it, so they can't disagree.
With @cuple/mcp, AI agents can call your routes as MCP tools. Like OpenAPI, it reads your routes from the TypeScript source. npm i -D @cuple/mcp typescript

// mcp.ts import { serveMcp } from "@cuple/mcp"; serveMcp("./src/routes.ts", "routes", { url: "http://localhost:8080/rpc" }); Then register it with your agent as a command. For example, in Claude Code: claude mcp add my-api -- npx tsx mcp.ts In this example: "routes" is the name of the exported variable that holds your routes, as for generateOpenAPI. Every route becomes a tool, named after the route, e.g. posts.getPost. .meta({ description }) becomes the tool's description. A tool's input is what the route declares: params, query, body and headers, the same as fetchCuple's. Tools call your running server at url, through the RPC endpoint, so routes without .path() work as well. The response is given back as JSON. If it's not success, the tool call is marked as an error. NOTE: serveMcp talks to the agent over stdin and stdout, so don't write logs to stdout in mcp.ts. NOTE: It reads your TypeScript source, so run it where the source is available.

The tools say what each route needs, headers included. With a login route and a route that requires authorization: login: builder .bodySchema(z.strictObject({ email: z.string(), password: z.string() })) .post(async ({ data }) => success({ token: await signIn(data.body) })), listPosts: builder .chain(authLink) // .headersSchema(z.looseObject({ authorization: z.string() })) .get(async () => success({ posts })), listPosts's tool requires headers.authorization, so the agent calls login with the credentials you give it, and sends the token it gets back with the gated calls. There's nothing to configure. NOTE: The token goes through the conversation, like anything the agent reads. Give an agent an account with only the access it needs.

createMcpServer takes the same arguments and returns the server without connecting it, for a transport of your own: import { createMcpServer } from "@cuple/mcp"; const server = createMcpServer("./src/routes.ts", "routes", { url: "http://localhost:8080/rpc" }); await server.connect(transport); // any transport from @modelcontextprotocol/sdk Why it works this way Tools call your running server. An agent gets the same validation, middlewares and auth as your app, so it can reach nothing a normal client can't. The route's types are the instructions. An agent learns that listPosts needs authorization the same way it learns it needs params, so logging in first follows from the types, with no extra setup to keep in sync.

Middlewares allow you to reuse logic by handling tasks like validation, access control, or response formatting. They offer several features: Passing data to other middlewares. Preventing further execution based on conditions. Sending responses, so you don't need to handle every case manually. Note: Schema validators are also treated as middlewares.

builder .middleware(async () => { const randomValue = Math.random(); if (randomValue > 0.5) return { next: true, randomValue }; return { next: false, statusCode: 500, message: "Unlucky" }; }) .get(async ({ data }) => { return success({ message: `You won with ${data.randomValue}`, }); }); In this example: If the middleware returns { next: true }, the execution proceeds to the next handler. You can also type-safely add data, as shown with randomValue in data.randomValue If the middleware returns { next: false }, it sends an immediate response, which requires a statusCode. It's recommended to include a result: 'some-error' as const for having a proper discriminated union in the response.

Some middlewares need to use data coming from schema validators. In order to use the data from the schema validation you have to keep the middleware function in the builder code. This, however, prevents you to just move the middleware function out of the builder. To solve this, Cuple introduces a wrapper called link, and you can connect links with each other. .buildLink() Creates a link from a build chain. Use this instead of the final middleware (get, post, ...). .chain(fooLink).chain(barLink) to bring multiple links into the build chain

const authLink = builder .headersSchema( z.looseObject({ authorization: z.string(), }) ) .middleware(async ({ data }) => { if (data.headers.authorization === "foo") return { next: true, }; return { next: false, statusCode: 401 as const, }; }) .buildLink(); const routes = { getAuthedWelcomeMessage: builder .chain(authLink) .get(async () => { return success({ message: "hi" }); }), };
Middlewares can depend on the output of previous middlewares. For example, a role-check middleware might depend on the result of an authentication middleware.

const authLink = builder .middleware(async () => ({ next: true, auth: { userId: 12345 } })) .buildLink(); const adminRoleLink = builder .expectChain<typeof authLink>() .middleware(async ({ data }) => { const user = await getUser(data.auth.userId) if(user.role !== 'admin') { return { next: false, statusCode: 403, message: "This is admin only." } } return { next: true, user } }) .buildLink(); return { someRoute: builder .chain(authLink) .chain(adminRoleLink) .get(async ({ data }) => { return success({ message: `You have access! Good ${data.user.name}` }); }), }; In this example: adminRoleLink depends on the output of authLink.

In more complex applications, middleware may need additional services like a database or external APIs. To keep the code maintainable and testable, it's best to inject these dependencies rather than import them directly. You can achieve this by creating middleware link factories.

function createAuthLink(builder: CupleBuilder) { return builder .middleware(async () => ({ next: true, auth: { userId: 12345 } })) .buildLink() } type AuthLink = ReturnType<typeof createAuthLink> function createAdminRoleLink(builder: CupleBuilder, userRepository: UserRepository) { return builder .expectChain<AuthLink>() .middleware(async ({ data }) => { const user = await getUser(data.auth.userId) if(user.role !== 'admin') { return { next: false, statusCode: 403, message: "Admins only." } } return { next: true, user } }) .buildLink() } function createAdminModule(builder: CupleBuilder, userRepository: UserRepository) { const authLink = createAuthLink(builder); const adminRoleLink = createAdminRoleLink(builder, userRepository); return { someRoute: builder .chain(authLink) .chain(adminRoleLink) .get(async ({ data }) => { return success({ message: `You have access! Good ${data.user.name}` }); }), }; } note: CupleBuilder is an exported type from the index.ts file Why it works this way Middlewares return data instead of attaching it to req. req.user set by a middleware is invisible to TypeScript, and a route that forgot the middleware still compiles. Returned data is typed in data, and exists only on routes that chain the middleware.
Adding every routes in one file can be hard to do. Luckily, you don't have to.

const authModule = { login: /*...*/, register: /*...*/, } const postsModule = { getPost: /*...*/, getPosts: /*...*/, createPost: /*...*/, deletePost: /*...*/, } const app = { auth: authModule, posts: postsModule, } export type Routes = typeof app; Deeply nesting modules is also supported.
Cuple lets you do it your way, but if you are unsure here's an example: Usually it make sense to have createSomeModule function that initializes the module with all of its dependencies and routes.

// index.ts const routes = { auth: createAuthModule(db, builder), }; // modules/auth/index.ts export function createAuthModule(db: PrismaClient, builder: Builder) { return { login: builder.post(async ({data}) => { /* login */ }), register: builder.post(async ({data}) => { /* register */ }), // ... }; }

Since Cuple is REST compatible, you can generate an OpenAPI 3.0 spec from your routes. It reads your TypeScript source at build time, so there's nothing to add at runtime. npm i -D @cuple/openapi typescript

// routes.ts export const routes = { getPost: builder .path("/api/posts/:id") .paramsSchema(z.strictObject({ id: z.coerce.number() })) .get(async ({ data }) => { const post = await getPost(data.params.id); if (!post) return apiResponse("not-found", 404, { message: "Post not found" }); return success({ post }); }), createPost: builder .meta({ description: "Creates a new blog post" }) .path("/api/posts") .bodySchema(z.strictObject({ title: z.string(), content: z.string() })) .post(async ({ data }) => { return success({ id: 1 }); }), }; // scripts/openapi.ts import { generateOpenAPI } from "@cuple/openapi"; generateOpenAPI("./src/routes.ts", "routes", { tsconfigPath: "./tsconfig.json", info: { title: "Blog API", version: "1.0.0" }, outputFile: "./openapi.json", }); In this example: "routes" is the name of the exported variable that holds your routes. /api/posts/:id becomes /api/posts/{id}. Every possible response is included, grouped by status code, so 404 not-found is in the spec as well. .meta({ description }) becomes the operation's description. The operation id is the name of the route, e.g. getPost, or posts.getPost if it's nested. NOTE: Only routes with .path() are included, the others are only reachable through the RPC endpoint. NOTE: generateOpenAPI returns the document as well, so outputFile is optional.

Cuple OpenAPI .path("/posts/:id") path /posts/{id} .get() / .post() / ... operation with that method .paramsSchema(...) path parameters .querySchema(...) query parameters .headersSchema(...) header parameters .bodySchema(...) application/json request body return values responses by status code .meta({ description }) description

@cuple/openapi is built on @cuple/inspect, which you can use directly if you need the route information for something else: import { inspectRoutes } from "@cuple/inspect"; for (const route of inspectRoutes("./src/routes.ts", "routes")) { console.log(route.method.toUpperCase(), route.path.raw); } Why it works this way Generated from the source. Hand-written specs and annotations drift from what the handlers return. Reading the same types the client uses keeps the spec true without extra code.

The normal handlers give you JSON responses only. You still have access to Request and Response objects, so you can set, for example, custom headers. However, if you need xml, binary, or any other kind of response, you can use raw handlers. builder.getRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.postRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.putRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.patchRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */}) builder.deleteRaw(async ({ req, res, data }) => {/* ... */})

Use raw handlers when you need: Non-JSON responses (XML, CSV, binary files, downloads) Streaming responses (Server-Sent Events, file streams) Feature Normal Handlers Raw Handlers Response format JSON only Any format Error handling Automatic Manual Client support @cuple/client, fetch fetch

With normal handlers, if a middleware fails (returns { next: false }), the error response is automatically sent back as JSON. You don’t need to handle it manually. With raw handlers, this automatic behavior is disabled. The data object passed into the raw handler contains both success and error responses of your middlewares. That means you must explicitly send both success and error responses of your middlewares yourself.

builder .path("/test") .middleware(async () => { if (Math.random() < 0.5) { // success case: continue return { next: true, bar: "hey", }; } // failure case: stop execution return { next: false, statusCode: 400, foo: "hello", }; }) .getRaw(async ({ res, data }) => { if (data.next === false) { // middleware blocked -> manual error response res.status(data.statusCode).send(data.foo); } else { // middleware passed -> manual success response res.status(200).send(data.bar); } });

Cuple uses Express under the hood, giving you full access to req and res objects. With raw handlers, all automatic behavior is disabled, allowing you to use Express as designed while benefiting from Cuple's type-safe composition features. Please check express tutorials for more. Why it works this way Raw handlers are separate. A file download or a CSV isn't a typed result. Keeping them in their own handlers keeps every other route fully typed, instead of widening all responses to "anything".

client.with({ ... }) returns a client that adds the same data to every request, like an authorization header. const client = createClient<typeof routes>({ path: "http://localhost:8080/rpc", }); const authedClient = client.with({ middleware: () => ({ headers: { authorization: localStorage.getItem("token") || "nothing" }, }), }); // GOOD: await fetchCuple(authedClient.getProfile.get); // ALSO GOOD: await fetchCuple(client.getProfile.get, { headers: { authorization: localStorage.getItem("token") || "nothing" }, }); // A route that requires the header, called without it, is a type error: await fetchCuple(client.getProfile.get); // TYPE ERROR

Option Runs For middleware Before every request; awaited, so it can refresh a token. Data every request needs: headers, a tenant id. key When a cache needs it (a string, or a synchronous getter). Telling caches whose data a response is. See Switching and signing out. finalware After every response, before it's handed back. Cross-cutting reactions: redirect on an expired session, report failures. Throwing turns a result into an exception. NOTE: key is what the response depends on (who the user is), not the injected bytes (the token). A refreshed token is the same user. NOTE: finalware can replace the response, but the types don't follow it. Observe or throw; don't reshape. Why it works this way Required headers are part of the type. A forgotten auth header is otherwise a 401 found in production. When the route's schema requires it, a call without it doesn't compile. middleware runs per request. Tokens expire. Reading the token when the request is sent means a long-lived client never sends a stale one. key is separate from middleware. A cache can't see what middleware injects, and the token changes while the user doesn't. Naming the identity keeps cached data apart per account, without discarding it on every token refresh.

Here's a very basic request handler: builder.get(async () => { return { result: 'success' as const, statusCode: 200 as const, message: "Hey!" } }) The builder is the request handler builder that you've created during the installation. The .get sets the final middleware with the appropriate HTTP method. The supported methods are: get, post, put, patch, delete The async () => { /* ... */ } is the function where your controller logic leaves The return type should contain these fields: result: a unique const indentifier for each possible responses. statusCode: the HTTP status code. For client-side typing it needs to be const as well.

Adding result and statusCode manually can be noisy. It's advised to create factory methods for common response types like success. success is included in the package: import { success } from '@cuple/server' builder.get(async () => { return success({ message: "Hey!" }) }) Cuple needs validationErrors internally, so you can access these as well: import { validationError } from '@cuple/server' builder.get(async () => { return validationError({ message: "We found some issues with your request" }) }) import { zodValidationError } from '@cuple/server' builder.get(async () => { return zodValidationError([{ code: "custom", path: ["password2"], message: "Passwords do not match.", }]); }) And there's also a generic apiResponse method, so you don't have to keep track the shape of the return type: import { apiResponse } from '@cuple/server' builder.get(async () => { return apiResponse("not-found-error", 404, { message: "Resource not found", }); }) Example for custom factory method: export function notFoundError(others?: {message: string}) { return apiResponse("not-found-error", 404, { message: others?.message || "Resource not found", }); }

The first argument is an object containing 3 elements: req: Express' Request object res: Express' Response object data: custom data from the middlewares builder .chain(auth) .bodySchema( z.strictObject({ oldPassword: z.string(), password1: z.string().min(6), password2: z.string().min(6), }), ) .post(async ({ req, res, data }) => { // You can access request object req.body // but you have better, type-safe way to deal with the incoming data data.body.password1 }) Why it works this way A result next to the status code. Status codes are too coarse to branch on: a 404 can mean "no such route" or "no such order". A result names the outcome, and TypeScript narrows by it. Handlers return instead of calling res.send. Only a returned value is in the handler's type, and so in the client's. A response sent by hand is invisible to both.

Instead of returning one response, you can stream events with an async generator. Every yielded object is sent to the client as an event. The supported methods are: getSSE, postSSE, putSSE, patchSSE, deleteSSE

builder .chain(authLink) .getSSE(async function* ({ data, disconnectSignal }) { for await (const event of activityFeed.subscribe(disconnectSignal)) { yield { action: event.action, by: data.account.name }; } }); In this example: Middlewares run first. If one of them fails, the client gets a normal JSON error response. When the client disconnects, the generator is stopped, and disconnectSignal is aborted.

const stream = await fetchCupleSSE(client.activity.get, {}); for await (const event of stream) { console.log(event.by, event.action); } In React, use useStream. NOTE: If your generator ends on its own, and it should finish even without the client, use getSSE(generator, { returnOnDisconnect: false }). Never do this with an endless loop. Why it works this way Middlewares run before the stream opens. Once an event stream has started, an error can't change the HTTP status. Running auth and validation first means a rejection is a normal JSON result, handled like any failed request. Generators stop on disconnect. A client that navigates away would otherwise leave a subscription or a loop running on the server.

Cuple uses Zod for schema validation. It was choosen because of the good defaults and the great type inference. Within Cuple the ZodIssue is also extended for additional type-safety. You can validate, parse, and convert each part of an HTTP request.

Internally it parses express' req.headers object, so you should use the same naming. Successfully parsed result will be added to data.headers. builder .headersSchema(z.looseObject({ authorization: z.string() })) .get(async ({ data }) => { data.headers.authorization // this has a string value });
Currently only json requests are supported. Successfully parsed result will be added to data.body. .bodySchema(z.strictObject({ user: z.strictObject({ name: z.string().min(3), age: z.number() }) }))

Note: Query parameters are always strings! Luckily zod can convert it to number if you use z.coerce.number(). Successfully parsed result will be added to data.query. // For URL query parsing (e.g.: ?somevar=12) .querySchema(z.strictObject({ somevar: z.coerce.number() }))

Note: Path parameters are always strings! Luckily zod can convert it to number if you use z.coerce.number(). Successfully parsed result will be added to data.body. // For URL params parsing .path("/post/:id") .paramsSchema(z.strictObject({ id: z.coerce.number() }))

In case of error Cuple sends a ZodValidationError error. An example response: { result: 'validation-error', statusCode: 422, message: "We found some incorrect field(s) during validating the form.", issues: [{ path: ["email"] message: 'This field is required.' code: 'invalid_type' }] } Why it works this way Invalid input is a normal result. A form sending bad input is expected, not exceptional. As a validation-error with paths, the client can put each message on its field, and the type says what the issues look like.
